title: Advanced STEM Analysis of Anion Void Lattice and Defects Evolution in Electron Irradiated CaF2
content: Void superlattices have been recognized as a distinct self-organization phenomenon in materials exposed to high-energy particle irradiation, wherein voids self-organize into three dimensional ordered structures that commensurate with the host matrix. This occurs under far-from-equilibrium conditions driven by a high defect production rate [1]. Unraveling the mechanism underlying this unique response to energetic particle irradiation is essential for understanding the process of formation and stability of irradiation-induced nanostructures in materials. Formation of void superlattice in electron irradiated (100 keV-1 MeV) calcium fluorite (CaF2) has been investigated using in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and the void lattice was found to have a simple cubic structure whose axes are commensurate with cubic fluorite matrix and anion sublattice [2, 3]. Conclusions were drawn based on these observations and optical absorption experiments, suggesting that the phenomenon is due to a radiolytic process with the anisotropic diffusion of F interstitials serving as the driving force. [2, 4]. Due to the previous lack of solid experimental evidence, a fundamental issue has persisted in interpreting the nature of these voids: are they completely devoid of atoms, or do they consist of Ca metallic colloids with complete fluoride depletion, thus qualifying as anion voids? Here, we present new findings from integrated electron microscopy using 200 keV scanning transmission electron microscopy annular dark field (STEM-ADF) imaging combined with EDS and EELS analyses.
